It describes the conduct of the scholar trained for public duty, the superior man, and the ways virtue, learning, righteousness, and mourning should be pursued. Tsze-hsia discusses teaching, confidence, study, and the limits of grief, while the philosopher Tsang comments on Tsze-chang, filial piety, and criminal judgment. Tsze-kung defends Chung-ni’s attainments, explains how the doctrines of Wan and Wu are preserved, and describes the effects of a sage’s rule.

l: Tsze-chang, The Analects of Confucius, Book XIX: Tsze-Chang, The Analects, Book XIX: Tsze-Chang / CHAP. I. Tsze-chang said, 'The scholar, trained for public duty, .. CHAP. XXV. 1. Ch'an Tsze-ch'in, addressing Tsze-kung, said,
s: Tsze-chang says that the scholar trained for public duty should sacrifice his life when danger threatens, think of righteousness when gain is offered, and be reverential in sacrifice and concerned with proper grief in mourning. He also asks about mutual intercourse and says that the superior man honors the talented and virtuous, bears with all, praises the good, and pities the incompetent.

l: Tsze-hsia, The Analects of Confucius, Book XIX: Tsze-Chang, The Analects, Book XIX: Tsze-Chang / CHAP. I. Tsze-chang said, 'The scholar, trained for public duty, .. CHAP. XXV. 1. Ch'an Tsze-ch'in, addressing Tsze-kung, said,
s: Tsze-hsia teaches that inferior studies may have value but should not be extended into remote applications. He says that learning requires daily recognition of what is not yet attained, remembrance of what has been gained, extensive study, sincere purpose, earnest inquiry, and self-applied reflection. He also teaches that confidence should precede imposing labors or remonstrating, and that mourning should stop when grief has reached its utmost degree.

l: the philosopher Tsang, The Analects of Confucius, Book XIX: Tsze-Chang, The Analects, Book XIX: Tsze-Chang / CHAP. I. Tsze-chang said, 'The scholar, trained for public duty, .. CHAP. XXV. 1. Ch'an Tsze-ch'in, addressing Tsze-kung, said,
s: The philosopher Tsang says that Tsze-chang has an imposing manner and is difficult to join in practicing virtue. He teaches that mourning for parents may reveal what people have not otherwise fully shown, praises Mang Chwang’s filial piety in preserving his father’s ministers and government, and tells Yang Fu to pity those found guilty rather than rejoice in his own ability.

l: Tsze-kung, The Analects of Confucius, Book XIX: Tsze-Chang, The Analects, Book XIX: Tsze-Chang / CHAP. I. Tsze-chang said, 'The scholar, trained for public duty, .. CHAP. XXV. 1. Ch'an Tsze-ch'in, addressing Tsze-kung, said,
s: Tsze-kung says that Chau’s wickedness was not as great as his reputation implies and that the superior man should avoid places where evil gathers. l: Chung-ni, The Analects of Confucius, Book XIX: Tsze-Chang, The Analects, Book XIX: Tsze-Chang / CHAP. I. Tsze-chang said, 'The scholar, trained for public duty, .. CHAP. XXV. 1. Ch'an Tsze-ch'in, addressing Tsze-kung, said,

s: The superior man honors the talented and virtuous, bears with all, praises the good, and pities the incompetent. He does not carry inferior studies into remote applications, undergoes changes in outward manner while remaining firm in speech, and has faults that all can see but also changes that cause all to look up to him.

l: the people, The Analects of Confucius, Book XIX: Tsze-Chang, The Analects, Book XIX: Tsze-Chang / CHAP. I. Tsze-chang said, 'The scholar, trained for public duty, .. CHAP. XXV. 1. Ch'an Tsze-ch'in, addressing Tsze-kung, said,
s: The people may be imposed labors upon after they have given their ruler confidence; without that confidence, they think themselves oppressed. Under the sage’s rule, the people would be established, follow their leader, become happy, resort to his dominions, and live harmoniously.

l: virtue, The Analects of Confucius, Book XIX: Tsze-Chang, The Analects, Book XIX: Tsze-Chang / CHAP. I. Tsze-chang said, 'The scholar, trained for public duty, .. CHAP. XXV. 1. Ch'an Tsze-ch'in, addressing Tsze-kung, said,
s: Virtue is associated with holding fast to it while enlarging it, believing right principles with firm sincerity, learning extensively with a sincere aim, inquiring earnestly, and reflecting with self-application. Tsze-kung says that other men’s talents and virtue are like hillocks and mounds, while Chung-ni is like the sun or moon.

s: Learning involves recognizing what has not yet been attained, remembering what has been attained, studying extensively, maintaining a firm and sincere aim, inquiring earnestly, and reflecting with self-application. The superior man learns to reach the utmost of his principles, and the student who completes learning should apply himself to be an officer.

s: In mourning, the scholar trained for public duty thinks about the grief he should feel. Tsze-hsia says that mourning should stop when grief has been carried to its utmost degree, and the philosopher Tsang says that mourning for parents may reveal a person’s full inner character.

s: The doctrines of Wan and Wu have not fallen to the ground and are found among men. Men of talents and virtue remember their greater principles, while others remember their smaller principles, so everyone possesses some part of them.

s: The sage’s rule is described as planting the people so that they are established, leading them so that they follow, making them happy so that multitudes resort to the dominions, and stimulating them so that they become harmonious. l: The Analects of Confucius, Book XX (Yao Yueh), The Analects of Confucius, Book XX (Yao Yueh), CHAP. I. 1. Yao said, 'Oh! you, Shun, the Heaven-determined

l: Yao, The Analects of Confucius, Book XX (Yao Yueh), CHAP. I. 1. Yao said, 'Oh! you, Shun, the Heaven-determined

s: Shun receives Yao's charge and uses the same language when giving charge to Yu.

s: T'ang announces before God that he does not dare pardon the sinner and that God's ministers are not kept in obscurity. He says that offences committed by him are not to be attributed to the people, while offences committed by the people rest on his person.

l: Chau, The Analects of Confucius, Book XX (Yao Yueh), CHAP. I. 1. Yao said, 'Oh! you, Shun, the Heaven-determined
s: Chau confers great gifts, enriches the good, and says that virtuous men are more important to him than near relatives. He restores measures, laws, officers, extinguished States, broken lines of succession, and retired people, while emphasizing food, mourning duties, and sacrifices. His generosity, sincerity, earnest activity, and justice win the people and make his achievements great.

l: Heaven, The Analects of Confucius, Book XX (Yao Yueh), CHAP. I. 1. Yao said, 'Oh! you, Shun, the Heaven-determined
s: Heaven determines the order of succession transferred to Shun. The Heavenly revenue will come to a perpetual end if there is distress and want within the four seas.

l: God, The Analects of Confucius, Book XX (Yao Yueh), CHAP. I. 1. Yao said, 'Oh! you, Shun, the Heaven-determined
s: God is addressed as the most great and sovereign God. T'ang says that God examines the sinner and ministers by God's mind, and that offences by the people rest on T'ang's person.

s: The due Mean is what Yao charges Shun to hold fast sincerely.

l: the people, The Analects of Confucius, Book XX (Yao Yueh), CHAP. I. 1. Yao said, 'Oh! you, Shun, the Heaven-determined
s: The people are held accountable through T'ang for offences committed in the myriad regions. Under Chau, their hearts turn toward him, they repose trust in him, and they are delighted by his justice.

l: good government of the kingdom, The Analects of Confucius, Book XX (Yao Yueh), CHAP. I. 1. Yao said, 'Oh! you, Shun, the Heaven-determined
s: Good government of the kingdom takes its course after Chau attends to weights and measures, examines the laws, and restores discarded officers.

l: the kingdom, The Analects of Confucius, Book XX (Yao Yueh), CHAP. I. 1. Yao said, 'Oh! you, Shun, the Heaven-determined
s: The kingdom is governed through restored laws, officers, States, families, and people who had retired into obscurity. Its welfare is tied to the food of the people, mourning duties, sacrifices, and the prevention of distress and want within the four seas.

l: The Analects of Confucius, Book XX (Yao Yueh), The Analects of Confucius, Book XX (Yao Yueh), CHAP. II. 1. Tsze-chang asked Confucius, saying, 'In what way
s: Tsze-chang asks Confucius how a person in authority can conduct government properly. Confucius teaches that the person in authority should honour five excellent things: beneficence without great expenditure, assigning proper tasks without causing repining, pursuing desires without covetousness, maintaining dignified ease without pride, and being majestic without fierceness. Confucius identifies four bad things: killing people without instruction, suddenly demanding full work without warning, enforcing previously non-urgent orders harshly, and giving pay or rewards stingily.

s: The four bad things are killing people without instruction, suddenly requiring the full tale of work without warning, enforcing orders harshly after first presenting them without urgency, and giving pay or rewards stingily.

s: The people benefit when the person in authority makes beneficial the things from which they naturally derive benefit. They do not repine when assigned proper labours, and they are harmed by sudden demands, uninstructed punishment, and harsh enforcement.

l: Propriety, The Analects of Confucius, Book XX (Yao Yueh), CHAP III. 1. The Master said, 'Without recognising the

l: rules of Propriety, The Analects of Confucius, Book XX (Yao Yueh), CHAP III. 1. The Master said, 'Without recognising the

s: Words have a force that must be known in order to know men.

l: The Great Learning, The Great Learning, The Great Learning / The Text of Confucius .. Chapter 10
s: The Great Learning teaches that people should illustrate illustrious virtue, renovate the people, and rest in the highest excellence through ordered stages of self-cultivation and government. The Text of Confucius explains that investigating things completes knowledge, sincere thoughts rectify the heart, and cultivation of the person regulates the family and state. Chapter 10 teaches that the sovereign gains or loses the kingdom through virtue and the people, while wealth must remain subordinate to righteousness. It also describes the virtuous minister, the production and use of wealth, and the dangers of favoritism, selfishness, and improper gain.

l: The Great Learning, The Great Learning, The Great Learning / The Text of Confucius .. Chapter 10
s: The Great Learning teaches the illustration of illustrious virtue, the renovation of the people, and resting in the highest excellence. It presents the cultivation of the person as the root of everything besides.

l: The Text of Confucius, The Great Learning, The Great Learning / The Text of Confucius .. Chapter 10
s: The Text of Confucius explains the ordered progression from investigating things and completing knowledge to sincere thoughts, a rectified heart, personal cultivation, family regulation, and proper government.

l: Confucius, The Great Learning, The Great Learning / The Text of Confucius .. Chapter 10
s: Confucius says that hearing litigations is not enough and that the people should be brought to have no litigations. He also teaches that a man should know where to rest.

l: the Great Learning’s teachings, The Great Learning, The Great Learning / The Text of Confucius .. Chapter 10
s: The Great Learning’s teachings require knowing what is first and last, cultivating the person, and treating that cultivation as the root of good order.

l: illustrious virtue, The Great Learning, The Great Learning / The Text of Confucius .. Chapter 10
s: Illustrious virtue is to be made manifest throughout the kingdom. The sovereigns mentioned in the unit made their virtue illustrious through their conduct.

l: the people, The Great Learning, The Great Learning / The Text of Confucius .. Chapter 10
s: The people are to be renovated, instructed, and made tranquil and happy. They follow rulers who lead with benevolence and righteousness, and their support determines whether the kingdom is gained or lost.

l: the kingdom, The Great Learning, The Great Learning / The Text of Confucius .. Chapter 10
s: The kingdom becomes tranquil and happy when states, families, persons, hearts, thoughts, and knowledge are properly ordered. It is gained by gaining the people and lost by losing them.

l: the state, The Great Learning, The Great Learning / The Text of Confucius .. Chapter 10
s: The state is properly governed after the family is regulated and the person cultivated. Its prosperity is found in righteousness rather than pecuniary gain.

l: the family, The Great Learning, The Great Learning / The Text of Confucius .. Chapter 10
s: The family is regulated through cultivation of the person and serves as the basis for teaching and governing the state. A ruler's family example influences the whole state.

l: the person, The Great Learning, The Great Learning / The Text of Confucius .. Chapter 10
s: The person is cultivated by rectifying the heart, making thoughts sincere, and extending knowledge through investigating things. From the Son of Heaven down to the mass of the people, cultivation of the person is the root of everything besides.

l: the heart, The Great Learning, The Great Learning / The Text of Confucius .. Chapter 10
s: The heart is rectified when thoughts are sincere and is disturbed by passion, terror, fond regard, sorrow, or distress. When the heart is not present, a person looks without seeing, hears without understanding, and eats without knowing the taste.

l: knowledge, The Great Learning, The Great Learning / The Text of Confucius .. Chapter 10
s: Knowledge is extended through the investigation of things and becomes complete when things have been investigated. Complete knowledge leads to sincere thoughts.

l: thoughts, The Great Learning, The Great Learning / The Text of Confucius .. Chapter 10
s: Thoughts are made sincere by allowing no self-deception and by being watchful over oneself when alone. Sincere thoughts lead to a rectified heart.

l: the Son of Heaven, The Great Learning, The Great Learning / The Text of Confucius .. Chapter 10
s: The Son of Heaven, like all people, must consider cultivation of the person the root of everything besides.

l: the sovereign, The Great Learning, The Great Learning / The Text of Confucius .. Chapter 10
s: The sovereign makes the people filial, brotherly, and compassionate by treating the aged, elders, and young and helpless properly. The sovereign gains the kingdom through the people and virtue, but loses it through a want of goodness.

l: the superior man, The Great Learning, The Great Learning / The Text of Confucius .. Chapter 10
s: The superior man uses his utmost endeavors, knows where to rest, and cultivates himself through learning and self-culture. He is watchful over himself when alone and makes his thoughts sincere.

l: the Book of Poetry, The Great Learning, The Great Learning / The Text of Confucius .. Chapter 10
s: The Book of Poetry is cited to teach resting, self-culture, reverence, remembrance of former kings, family order, and the proper conduct of rulers. Its passages also describe rulers as parents of the people and warn that the great decree is not easily preserved.

l: wealth, The Great Learning, The Great Learning / The Text of Confucius .. Chapter 10
s: Wealth is the result, while virtue is the root. Accumulating wealth scatters the people, whereas allowing wealth to be scattered among them collects the people; wealth should not be treated as the state's true prosperity.

l: the cultivation of the person, The Great Learning, The Great Learning / The Text of Confucius .. Chapter 10
s: The cultivation of the person depends on rectifying the heart and is the root of everything besides. It enables the regulation of the family and the proper government of the state.

l: the regulation of the family, The Great Learning, The Great Learning / The Text of Confucius .. Chapter 10
s: The regulation of the family depends on cultivation of the person and allows the ruler to teach the state through filial piety, fraternal submission, and kindness. A rightly ordered household provides an example for the people.

l: the government of the state, The Great Learning, The Great Learning / The Text of Confucius .. Chapter 10
s: The government of the state depends on the regulation of the family and on the ruler's own conduct. It makes the whole kingdom peaceful and happy when the ruler possesses good qualities and treats the people properly.

l: filial piety, The Great Learning, The Great Learning / The Text of Confucius .. Chapter 10
s: Filial piety is a quality through which the sovereign should be served. When the sovereign behaves properly toward the aged, the people become filial.

l: fraternal submission, The Great Learning, The Great Learning / The Text of Confucius .. Chapter 10
s: Fraternal submission is a quality through which elders and superiors should be served. When the sovereign behaves properly toward elders, the people learn brotherly submission.

l: benevolence, The Great Learning, The Great Learning / The Text of Confucius .. Chapter 10
s: Benevolence leads rulers such as Yao and Shun to be followed by the people. A sovereign who loves benevolence is associated with people who love righteousness.

l: the ruler’s virtue, The Great Learning, The Great Learning / The Text of Confucius .. Chapter 10
s: The ruler’s virtue is the root of the people, territory, wealth, and resources for expenditure. A virtuous ruler uses wealth to make himself more distinguished, while a vicious ruler accumulates wealth at the expense of his life.

l: the people’s righteousness, The Great Learning, The Great Learning / The Text of Confucius .. Chapter 10
s: The people’s righteousness supports the completion of the sovereign's affairs. A state's prosperity is found in righteousness rather than in wealth or pecuniary gain.

l: a minister, The Great Learning, The Great Learning / The Text of Confucius .. Chapter 10
s: A minister should be plain, sincere, upright, generous, able to bear and employ capable people, and free from jealousy. A minister who seeks imposts from the people is worse than one who robs the house of its revenues, and a jealous minister endangers the state.

l: the measuring-square principle, The Great Learning, The Great Learning / The Text of Confucius .. Chapter 10
s: The measuring-square principle requires a person not to impose on inferiors or superiors what he dislikes receiving himself. It is the principle by which the ruler regulates his conduct.

l: The Doctrine of the Mean, The Doctrine of the Mean, The Doctrine of the Mean / Chapter 1
s: The Doctrine of the Mean explains that Heaven confers what is called the Nature, and accordance with the Nature is called the Path of duty. It teaches that the Path of duty cannot be left and that the superior man remains watchful over himself, especially when alone. It describes Equilibrium as the state before pleasure, anger, sorrow, or joy arise, and Harmony as the state when those feelings act in their due degree. When Equilibrium and Harmony exist in perfection, a happy order prevails throughout heaven and earth, and all things are nourished and flourish.

l: The Doctrine of the Mean, The Doctrine of the Mean, The Doctrine of the Mean / Chapter 1
s: The Doctrine of the Mean explains the Nature, the Path of duty, the superior man, Equilibrium, and Harmony.

l: Heaven, The Doctrine of the Mean, The Doctrine of the Mean / Chapter 1
s: Heaven confers what is called the Nature.

l: nature, The Doctrine of the Mean, The Doctrine of the Mean / Chapter 1
s: Nature is what Heaven has conferred. An accordance with Nature is called the Path of duty.

l: the way of the superior man, The Doctrine of the Mean, The Doctrine of the Mean / Chapter 1
s: The Path of duty is an accordance with Nature, and its regulation is called Instruction. It may not be left for an instant.

l: the superior man, The Doctrine of the Mean, The Doctrine of the Mean / Chapter 1
s: The superior man does not wait until he sees things to be cautious or until he hears things to be apprehensive. He is watchful over himself when he is alone.

l: Equilibrium, The Doctrine of the Mean, The Doctrine of the Mean / Chapter 1
s: Equilibrium is the state of the mind when pleasure, anger, sorrow, and joy have not stirred. It is the great root from which all the human actings in the world grow.

l: Harmony, The Doctrine of the Mean, The Doctrine of the Mean / Chapter 1
s: Harmony occurs when pleasure, anger, sorrow, and joy have been stirred and act in their due degree. It is the universal path which all should pursue.

l: Heaven and Earth, The Doctrine of the Mean, The Doctrine of the Mean / Chapter 1
s: When Equilibrium and Harmony exist in perfection, a happy order prevails throughout heaven and earth.

l: happy order, The Doctrine of the Mean, The Doctrine of the Mean / Chapter 1
s: A happy order prevails throughout heaven and earth when Equilibrium and Harmony exist in perfection, and all things are nourished and flourish.

l: Chung-ni, The Doctrine of the Mean, Chapter 2
s: Chung-ni explains the difference between the superior man and the mean man in relation to the course of the Mean.

l: the superior man, The Doctrine of the Mean, Chapter 2
s: The superior man embodies the course of the Mean and always maintains the Mean because he is a superior man.

l: mean man, The Doctrine of the Mean, Chapter 2

l: the course of the Mean, The Doctrine of the Mean, Chapter 2

l: the Mean, The Doctrine of the Mean, Chapter 2
s: The superior man always maintains the Mean, while the mean man acts contrary to it.

s: The Master says that perfect virtue is according to the Mean and observes that it has long been rare among the people.

l: perfect virtue, The Doctrine of the Mean, Chapter 3
s: Perfect is described as the virtue which is according to the Mean.

l: the virtue according to the Mean, The Doctrine of the Mean, Chapter 3
s: The virtue according to the Mean is identified as perfect, but it is said to have been rare among the people for a long time.

l: people, The Doctrine of the Mean, Chapter 3

s: The Master explains why the path of the Mean is not followed or understood. He says that knowledgeable people and men of talents and virtue go beyond it, while stupid and worthless people do not reach it. He adds that although everyone eats and drinks, few can distinguish flavors.

l: The Master, The Doctrine of the Mean, Chapter 4
s: The Master explains why the path of the Mean is not followed or understood. He says that knowledgeable people and men of talents and virtue go beyond it, while stupid and worthless people do not reach it.

l: the Mean, The Doctrine of the Mean, Chapter 4
s: The path of the Mean is not walked in or understood by most people. The knowing and men of talents and virtue go beyond it, while the stupid and worthless do not come up to it.

l: flavors, The Doctrine of the Mean, Chapter 4
s: Flavors are eaten and drunk by everyone, but few people can distinguish them.

l: The Doctrine of the Mean, The Doctrine of the Mean, Chapter 5
s: The Master remarks on the path of the Mean. He says that the path is untrodden. The unit concerns the Master's lament about the neglected path of the Mean.

l: The Master, The Doctrine of the Mean, Chapter 5
s: The Master says, "Alas! How is the path of the Mean untrodden!"

l: the Mean, The Doctrine of the Mean, Chapter 5
s: The Mean has a path that the Master says is untrodden.

l: The Doctrine of the Mean, The Doctrine of the Mean, Chapter 6
s: The Master describes Shun as greatly wise. Shun loved questioning others and studying their words, even when they were shallow. He concealed what was bad in their words and displayed what was good. He grasped both extremes, determined the Mean, and employed it in the government of the people.

l: Shun, The Doctrine of the Mean, Chapter 6
s: Shun is described as greatly wise. He questioned others, studied their words, concealed what was bad, displayed what was good, determined the Mean from two extremes, and employed it in his government of the people.

l: the Mean, The Doctrine of the Mean, Chapter 6
s: The Mean was determined by Shun from two extremes and employed in his government of the people.

l: government of the people, The Doctrine of the Mean, Chapter 6
s: The government of the people was conducted by Shun through his employment of the Mean.

l: The Doctrine of the Mean, The Doctrine of the Mean, Chapter 7
s: The Master says that men claim to be wise. Yet when they are driven forward and caught in a net, trap, or pitfall, they do not know how to escape. He also says that when men choose the course of the Mean, they cannot keep it for a full month.

l: The Master, The Doctrine of the Mean, Chapter 7
s: The Master says that men claim to be wise but cannot escape when driven forward and caught in a net, trap, or pitfall. He also says that men cannot maintain the course of the Mean for a full month.

l: men, The Doctrine of the Mean, Chapter 7
s: Men say that they are wise. Yet when driven forward and caught in a net, trap, or pitfall, they do not know how to escape. When they choose the course of the Mean, they cannot keep it for a full month.

l: the Mean, The Doctrine of the Mean, Chapter 7
s: The Mean is a course that men may choose. Men are not able to keep to it for a full month.

l: the course of the Mean, The Doctrine of the Mean, Chapter 7
s: Men may choose the course of the Mean, but they are not able to keep it for a full month.

l: The Doctrine of the Mean, The Doctrine of the Mean, Chapter 8
s: The Master describes the manner of Hui. Hui chose the Mean and held firmly to what was good. He kept what was good as if wearing it on his breast and did not lose it.

l: Hui, The Doctrine of the Mean, Chapter 8
s: Hui chose the Mean. Whenever Hui got hold of what was good, he clasped it firmly as if wearing it on his breast and did not lose it.

l: the Mean, The Doctrine of the Mean, Chapter 8
s: The Mean was chosen by Hui.

l: good qualities (in others), The Doctrine of the Mean, Chapter 8
s: What was good was obtained and firmly clasped by Hui, who did not lose it.

l: The Doctrine of the Mean, The Doctrine of the Mean, Chapter 9
s: The Master states that a kingdom, its states, and its families may be perfectly ruled. He says that dignities and emoluments may be declined. He also says that naked weapons may be trampled under the feet. Despite these achievements, he teaches that the course of the Mean cannot be attained to.

l: The Master, The Doctrine of the Mean, Chapter 9
s: The Master teaches that a kingdom, its states, and its families may be perfectly ruled, dignities and emoluments may be declined, and naked weapons may be trampled under the feet. He says that the course of the Mean cannot be attained to.

l: the Mean, The Doctrine of the Mean, Chapter 9
s: The Mean is presented as something whose course cannot be attained to, even when other difficult achievements are possible.

l: the course of the Mean, The Doctrine of the Mean, Chapter 9
s: The course of the Mean cannot be attained to, despite the possibility of perfectly ruling a kingdom, its states, and its families, declining dignities and emoluments, and trampling naked weapons under the feet.

l: The Doctrine of the Mean, The Doctrine of the Mean, Chapter 10
s: Tsze-lu asks the Master about energy. The Master distinguishes the energy of southern regions, northern regions, and the energy one should cultivate oneself. Southern energy consists of forbearance, gentleness, and not taking revenge, while northern energy consists of readiness for death without regret. The superior man cultivates friendly harmony without weakness and remains firm and unchanging whether good or bad principles prevail in government.

l: Tsze-lu, The Doctrine of the Mean, Chapter 10
s: Tsze-lu asks the Master about energy.

l: The Master, The Doctrine of the Mean, Chapter 10
s: The Master explains three forms of energy: the energy of southern regions, the energy of northern regions, and the energy one should cultivate oneself. He teaches that southern energy involves forbearance and gentleness without revenge, while northern energy involves lying under arms and meeting death without regret.

l: energy, The Doctrine of the Mean, Chapter 10
s: Energy may refer to the forbearance and gentleness studied by the good man, the readiness to meet death studied by the forceful, or the firm energy cultivated by the superior man. Firm energy includes maintaining one's course without changing when good or bad principles prevail in the country.

l: the superior man, The Doctrine of the Mean, Chapter 10
s: The superior man cultivates friendly harmony without weakness and stands firmly in the middle without inclining to either side. He does not change from what he was in retirement when good principles prevail, and he maintains his course to death when bad principles prevail.

l: The Doctrine of the Mean, The Doctrine of the Mean, Chapter 11
s: The Master describes what he does not do and what he cannot do. He does not live in obscurity while practicing wonders to gain honor in future ages. The good man tries to follow the right path but abandons it halfway, while the Master says he cannot stop in that way. The superior man follows the course of the Mean without regret even when unknown and unregarded, and only the sage is capable of this.

l: The Master, The Doctrine of the Mean, Chapter 11
s: The Master says that he does not live in obscurity and practice wonders to gain honor in future ages. He also says that, unlike the good man, he is not able to abandon the right path after going halfway.

l: the good man, The Doctrine of the Mean, Chapter 11
s: The good man tries to proceed according to the right path but abandons it when he has gone halfway.

l: the way of the superior man, The Doctrine of the Mean, Chapter 11
s: The right path is what the good man tries to follow before abandoning it halfway.

l: the superior man, The Doctrine of the Mean, Chapter 11
s: The superior man accords with the course of the Mean. Even when all unknown and unregarded by the world, he feels no regret.

l: the course of the Mean, The Doctrine of the Mean, Chapter 11
s: The course of the Mean is followed by the superior man, who accords with it without regret despite being unknown and unregarded.

l: the sage, The Doctrine of the Mean, Chapter 11
s: The sage is the only one able to remain without regret when following the course of the Mean while being unknown and unregarded.

l: The Doctrine of the Mean, The Doctrine of the Mean, Chapter 12
s: The way of the superior man reaches wide and far while remaining secret. Common men and women may understand and practice parts of it, though even the sage cannot fully know or carry it out. Its greatness cannot be fully embraced, and its minuteness cannot be divided. It appears above and below, in Heaven and earth and in the everyday intercourse of common men and women.

l: the way of the superior man, The Doctrine of the Mean, Chapter 12
s: It reaches wide and far while remaining secret. Its simple elements may be found in the intercourse of common men and women, while its utmost reaches shine through Heaven and earth. Even the sage cannot fully know or practice it.

l: the superior man, The Doctrine of the Mean, Chapter 12
s: He pursues a way that extends broadly and deeply. If he described it in its greatness, nothing could embrace it; if he described it in its minuteness, nothing could split it.

l: common men and women, The Doctrine of the Mean, Chapter 12
s: They may understand and practice parts of the way of the superior man, despite ignorance or being below the ordinary standard of character. The way may be found in their everyday intercourse.

l: The Doctrine of the Mean, The Doctrine of the Mean, Chapter 13
s: The Master explains that the path remains close to ordinary human consciousness and conduct. He teaches that the superior man governs people according to their nature, corrects what is wrong, and practices reciprocity by not doing to others what he would dislike for himself. He describes four standards of service and friendship that he has not yet attained. The superior man is marked by earnest practice, careful speech, and entire sincerity between words and actions.

l: The Master, The Doctrine of the Mean, Chapter 13
s: The Master teaches that the path is not far from ordinary human consciousness and that conduct distant from it cannot be considered the path. He describes the superior man's governance, reciprocity, standards of service, and entire sincerity.

l: the way of the superior man, The Doctrine of the Mean, Chapter 13
s: The path is not far from man and is connected with the common indications of consciousness. A course far from those indications cannot be considered the path.

l: the superior man, The Doctrine of the Mean, Chapter 13
s: The superior man governs people according to their nature and stops correcting them when they change what is wrong. He practices reciprocity, strives to serve others as he would have them serve him, and ensures that his words correspond to his actions.

l: reciprocity, The Doctrine of the Mean, Chapter 13
s: Reciprocity is described as exercising the principles of one's nature and not doing to others what one does not like done to oneself. It is part of the way of the superior man.

l: sincerity, The Doctrine of the Mean, Chapter 13
s: Entire sincerity marks the superior man when his words respect his actions and his actions respect his words. He is careful in speaking and does not permit excess in his words.

l: The Doctrine of the Mean, The Doctrine of the Mean, Chapter 14
s: The unit concerns the superior man and how he conducts himself in every station and circumstance. He does what is proper to his position, remains himself, and neither despises inferiors nor seeks favor from superiors. He rectifies himself, seeks nothing from others, and does not murmur against Heaven or grumble against men. He waits quietly for the appointments of Heaven, and when he fails, he looks within himself for the cause.

l: the superior man, The Doctrine of the Mean, Chapter 14
s: The superior man does what is proper to whatever station he occupies, remaining himself in wealth, poverty, among barbarous tribes, and in sorrow or difficulty. He does not despise inferiors or court superiors, but rectifies himself and seeks nothing from others. He waits quietly for the appointments of Heaven, and when he misses the center of the target, he seeks the cause of his failure in himself.

l: Heaven, The Doctrine of the Mean, Chapter 14
s: Heaven makes appointments that the superior man quietly waits for. The superior man does not murmur against Heaven.

l: The Doctrine of the Mean, The Doctrine of the Mean, Chapter 15
s: The chapter compares the way of the superior man to traveling a distance by first crossing the nearby space and to ascending a height by beginning on lower ground. It describes happy union with wife and children as musical harmony and concord among brethren as delightful and enduring harmony. The passage says that such harmony allows a family to be regulated and brings pleasure to a wife and children. The Master says that in such a state, parents have entire complacence.

l: the superior man, The Doctrine of the Mean, Chapter 15
s: The superior man is associated with a way that begins with what is near or lower before reaching what is distant or high.

l: the way of the superior man, The Doctrine of the Mean, Chapter 15
s: The way of the superior man is compared to traveling and ascending: one first traverses the space that is near and begins from the lower ground.

l: family, The Doctrine of the Mean, Chapter 15
s: The family may be regulated through happy union with wife and children and concord among brethren.

l: The Master, The Doctrine of the Mean, Chapter 15
s: The Master says that when such harmony exists, parents have entire complacence.

l: parents, The Doctrine of the Mean, Chapter 15
s: Parents have entire complacence when there is happy union with wife and children and concord among brethren.

l: The Doctrine of the Mean, The Doctrine of the Mean, Chapter 16
s: The Master explains how spiritual beings display their powers even though people cannot see or hear them. They enter into all things and influence people to fast, purify themselves, and dress richly for sacrifices. During worship, they seem to surround the worshippers above, to the right, and to the left. The passage teaches that the spirits’ subtle presence and the outgoings of sincerity cannot be repressed.

l: The Master, The Doctrine of the Mean, Chapter 16
s: The Master teaches that spiritual beings display abundant powers despite being unseen and unheard. He explains that they enter into all things, influence people to prepare for sacrifices, and appear to surround worshippers.

l: spiritual beings, The Doctrine of the Mean, Chapter 16
s: Spiritual beings display powers that people cannot see or hear, yet they enter into all things and are present everywhere. They cause people to fast, purify themselves, and dress richly for sacrifices, then seem to be above and beside their worshippers.

l: sacrifices, The Doctrine of the Mean, Chapter 16
s: Sacrifices are attended by people who fast, purify themselves, and array themselves in their richest dresses. Spiritual beings appear to surround those attending the sacrifices.

l: sincerity, The Doctrine of the Mean, Chapter 16
s: The passage teaches that the outgoings of sincerity cannot be repressed. Its manifestness is compared with the evident yet subtle presence of spiritual beings.

l: The Doctrine of the Mean, The Doctrine of the Mean, Chapter 17
s: The Master praises Shun as greatly filial and possessing the virtue of a sage. Shun had the throne, riches within the four seas, fame, and long life, and his descendants preserved sacrifices to him. Heaven is said to reward beings according to their qualities, nourishing what flourishes and overthrowing what is ready to fall. The unit concludes that a person of great virtue will surely receive the appointment of Heaven.

l: The Master, The Doctrine of the Mean, Chapter 17
s: The Master praises Shun as greatly filial and says that Shun possessed the virtue of a sage. He teaches that Heaven rewards great virtue with the appointment of Heaven.

l: Shun, The Doctrine of the Mean, Chapter 17
s: Shun is described as greatly filial and possessing the virtue of a sage. He held the throne, had riches within the four seas, received fame, attained long life, and had sacrifices preserved by his descendants.

l: Heaven, The Doctrine of the Mean, Chapter 17
s: Heaven is said to be bountiful to beings according to their qualities. It nourishes what is flourishing, overthrows what is ready to fall, and grants dignity and the throne as favors.

l: Shun's virtue, The Doctrine of the Mean, Chapter 17
s: Shun's virtue was that of a sage. Because of his great virtue, he obtained the throne, riches, fame, and long life.

l: throne, The Doctrine of the Mean, Chapter 17
s: The throne was obtained by Shun because of his great virtue. Heaven is said to decree the throne as one of its favors.

l: the appointments of Heaven, The Doctrine of the Mean, Chapter 17
s: The appointment of Heaven is received by one who is greatly virtuous. The Master presents this as a certainty.

l: The Doctrine of the Mean, The Doctrine of the Mean, Chapter 18
s: The unit concerns King Wan, King Chi, King Wu, and the duke of Chau in the establishment and transmission of royal dignity. King Wan is praised as having no cause for grief because his father was King Chi and his son was King Wu. King Wu continued the enterprise of King T'ai, King Chi, and King Wan, gained possession of the kingdom, and established royal succession and ancestral sacrifices. The duke of Chau completed the virtuous course of Wan and Wu and set rules for titles, sacrifices, burials, and mourning.

l: King Wan, The Doctrine of the Mean, Chapter 18
s: King Wan is described as having no cause for grief. His father was King Chi, and his son was King Wu; the duke of Chau completed his virtuous course.

l: King Chi, The Doctrine of the Mean, Chapter 18
s: King Chi was the father of King Wan. King Wu continued the enterprise of King Chi, along with that of King T'ai and King Wan.

l: King Wu, The Doctrine of the Mean, Chapter 18
s: King Wu was the son of King Wan. He continued the enterprise of King T'ai, King Chi, and King Wan, gained possession of the kingdom, received the royal throne, and established ancestral sacrifices maintained by his descendants.

l: duke of Chau, The Doctrine of the Mean, Chapter 18
s: The duke of Chau completed the virtuous course of Wan and Wu. He gave the title of king to T'ai and Chi, extended royal sacrificial rules through the kingdom, and established rules for burial, sacrifice, and mourning.

l: kingdom, The Doctrine of the Mean, Chapter 18
s: King Wu gained possession of the kingdom. The kingdom included princes, great officers, scholars, and common people to whom the duke of Chau extended the rules of royal ceremonies.

l: mourning, The Doctrine of the Mean, Chapter 18
s: One year's mourning was extended only to the great officers, while three years' mourning extended to the Son of Heaven. In mourning for a father or mother, no difference was allowed between the noble and the mean.

l: The Doctrine of the Mean, The Doctrine of the Mean, Chapter 19
s: The Master explains the far-reaching filial piety of King Wu and the duke of Chau. Filial piety consists in carrying out the wishes of forefathers and carrying forward their undertakings through ancestral ceremonies, offerings, music, and reverence. These ceremonies distinguish rank, descent, talents, worth, and age while serving the dead as if they were alive. Understanding the sacrifices to Heaven and Earth and the sacrifices to ancestors makes governing a kingdom as easy as looking into one’s palm.

l: The Master, The Doctrine of the Mean, Chapter 19
s: The Master teaches that the filial piety of King Wu and the duke of Chau was far-reaching. He explains the ceremonies and sacrifices through which filial piety is practiced and says that understanding them makes government easy.

l: King Wu, The Doctrine of the Mean, Chapter 19
s: King Wu is presented as having far-reaching filial piety. His filial piety is expressed through carrying out the wishes of forefathers and carrying forward their undertakings.

l: duke of Chau, The Doctrine of the Mean, Chapter 19
s: The duke of Chau is presented as having far-reaching filial piety. His filial piety is expressed through carrying out the wishes of forefathers and carrying forward their undertakings.

l: filial piety, The Doctrine of the Mean, Chapter 19
s: Filial piety is seen in skillfully carrying out the wishes of forefathers and carrying forward their undertakings. It is practiced through ancestral ceremonies, offerings, music, reverence, and love.

l: forefathers, The Doctrine of the Mean, Chapter 19
s: Forefathers are served through the occupation of their places, the practice of their ceremonies, and the performance of their music. Their wishes are carried out and their undertakings are carried forward.

l: ancestral temple, The Doctrine of the Mean, Chapter 19
s: The ancestral temple is the place where ancestral ceremonies distinguish the royal kindred according to descent and where sacrifices to ancestors are performed. Its ceremonies also distinguish rank, talents, worth, and age.

l: God, The Doctrine of the Mean, Chapter 19
s: God is served by means of the ceremonies of the sacrifices to Heaven and Earth.

l: Heaven and Earth, The Doctrine of the Mean, Chapter 19
s: Heaven and Earth are associated with sacrifices through whose ceremonies God is served.
